Never claimed they did :) . And this is an even longer debate to be honest. France, like every country in the world these days but especially “rich” country, is getting older. And “older” folk vote more and are likelier to be part of a union. So the unions (and the politician) have had more incentive to focus on the older part of the French population. Union also focus on worker rights, not people who never worked, which mean that youth with almost 0 job experience was always a blind spot for them (there is students unions and such, but it's another thing too). Not that they don't anything about that, but they don't defend as heavily young worker as they do for retirement benefit…

But whatever. No system is ever perfect, and I am certainly not claiming it is. But perfection is the enemy of progress. I was pointing out that the previous comment was an incomplete vision of what unions can do with layoff.

> Unions don’t stop layoffs, they just change who gets laid off to be less economical for the firm. Generally that means younger, more productive workers are let go ahead of senior, less productive ones. [GP]

> As an example, in France, the unions are often helping to negotiate the terms of the layoff to ensure… [OP]

The youth unemployment rate in France for 14-24 year olds is near 20%. [1]

Are you sure that unions are doing enough to help and protect young workers?

[1] https://www.wsj.com/economy/these-charts-show-why-young-peop...

Union can do way more than this. As an example, in France, the unions are often helping to negotiate the terms of the layoff to ensure :

- That employee can be requalified, re-trained, re-located, if possible and wanted instead of straight up laid off

- That laid off employees can benefit from paid training to help them find a job after being laid off

- The compensation for volunteers who choose to get laid off first

- And many other things

(note that unions in France are organized very differently than in the U.S and have different incentives)

A lot of time, they act as a “moderation” force between the will of the shareholders and the employees. They cannot really change the economical reality. And even if a company doing well but want to make pretty number before selling chunks of the company, there are many ways to do this. The union often ensure that they can't take measure that are too drastic with important human cost.

children.author: antihipocrat
children.text:
Profit is value generated by workers' time and effort that is being allocated elsewhere.

A business that has operating expenses equal to revenue is not withholding anything. One option available in this case is for workers to improve their productivity, no loss of jobs are necessary if there are market opportunities available. What better incentive is there for workers to improve their productivity than to share in the benefits of that improvement.

Also, a pay scale is a policy set by the business. Individual employees working at a level subject to scales like these have no influence on what these scales are, unions however spend a lot of time negotiating these scales with businesses. The C-suite captures a lot of value (CEOs now earn +300x more than the typical worker), this is a wage, and included operating expenses, that gap could come down quite a lot without impacting on the executive's lifestyle...

>You should unionize and negotiate for better terms, no matter how good your terms are already

A business only has a fixed amount of money it can spend on wages. Unionizing is not going to bring it up if you're already near the top of the pay scale for your role, and if it brings the wages of your lower-paid colleagues up then that means there'll be less left to pay those at the top so the wages of top earners will come down.

children.author: vld_chk
children.text:
I agree with your core idea that we should abandon our rose-tinted dreams of an eternally peaceful world and make sure we are well-equipped to protect the world we value.

However, the leap from “we should be ready to defend ourselves” to “therefore, we should allow Google to enter into unethical contracts and develop hostile, superintelligent AI capable of destroying us” is much harder to justify.

The fundamental flaw in this argument is: how can we guarantee that Google or any other lab will weaponize AI in our interests? How do we control it? How do we ensure that it won’t be turned into a weapon of surveillance and control against us and domestic political opposition? We live in an era of unprecedented economic inequality, with politicians increasingly relying on oligarchic wealth and unethical practices to win votes.

Therefore, the strategic solution cannot simply be “let’s pretend we don’t need weapons.” I agree that thinking otherwise is delusional. But until we have proper guardrails in place and meaningful oversight of frontier AI labs, organizing unions and pushing for slower development and tighter controls is a better approach than simply closing our eyes and hoping that Google executives know what they’re doing.

children.author: impossiblefork

All the major blocks have nuclear weapons though, so this island situation isn't really applicable.

Things like surveillance, spying, methods that can figure out what people are thinking and doing are also something which can enable the apparent stabilization of genuinely unstable societies, such as can be created by mass immigration and the like, so it isn't clear that developing these things for intelligence or military applications will bring order or strengthen society-- it can instead become a means whereby society is able to function while operating in a manner which will eventually destroy it utterly.

Finally, if AI is to be used for warfare, and this to be beneficial to society-- i.e. strengthen the internally peaceful island which still prepares for war. Present wars have not however had this character. Nicaragua is certainly not inimical to the EU-- Iran is, but not in a manner that makes it reasonable to destabilize it, Iraq, Afghanistan, etc. certainly weren't. The one war we have is the Russian war, and there what use is AI really? I see the interesting things as increase the strike range of drones and things that have very little to do with frontier LLMs or the sort of work that DeepMind is famous for.

So I actually think your remark while perhaps true in many other contexts is absolutely wrong in this context. I think Britain is better off if DeepMind stays out of supplying weapons or surveillance technology whether to the US or anybody else.
